sentences.text: Baurusuchus was a terrestrial carnivore that lived in a hot and arid climate.
This predator is estimated to have weighed up to 113.4 kilograms.
Adults measured between 3.5 and 4 meters in length.
The species B. salgadoensis generated a bite force between 2542 and 3088 Newtons, which is considerable for its size.
This power is comparable to that of the American alligator.
Unlike modern crocodilians, its external nostrils were not adapted for an amphibious lifestyle.
The genus Baurusuchus was first described by Price in 1945.
Price also named the type species B. pachecoi in that same year.
Later, Carvalho et al. named the species B. salgadoensis in 2005.
Nascimento and Zaher named the species B. albertoi in 2010.
It likely hunted by ambushing prey and pulling back with serrated, blade-like teeth.
Enlarged and strongly bent pterygoids allowed it to close its jaw very quickly using powerful muscles.
The animal may have shaken prey violently with its jaws, aided by enlarged cervical neural spines.
It likely dug holes to find water during dry seasons or for thermoregulation.
Baurusuchus likely competed with abelisaurid dinosaurs for food in its ecosystem.
Although the highly curved pterygoid suggests a rapid bite, this bite was somewhat weak.
Baurusuchus is the type genus of the family Baurusuchidae.
This family includes crocodiliforms with elongated and laterally compressed skulls.
A 2011 study established a new subfamily called Baurusuchinae.
The subfamily Baurusuchinae includes only Stratiotosuchus and Baurusuchus.
A 2014 study referred a new species, Aplestosuchus sordidus, to the subfamily.
However, that study considered B. albertoi a close relative of Aplestosuchus instead.
Baurusuchus lived in Brazil between 90 and 83.5 million years ago during the Late Cretaceous period.
Other estimates place its time range from the Campanian to the Maastrichtian stages, between 83.6 and 66 million years ago.
Some researchers do not support the affiliation of B. albertoi to Baurusuchus.
